FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 25th, 1887.

The Convention was called to order at 12 m. by Bro. Bridgman, President.
The minutes of the previous sessions were read and approved.
Bro. Bayliss (A) offered Gen. Res. No. VI, which, under a suspension of the
rules, was immediately voted upon and unanimously adopted.
Bro. Burpee (K), for the Committee on the Annual Communication of the
Executive Council, reported General Resolutions Nos. II, III and VII, and
special resolutions Nos. I, II and HI, which were unanimously adopted.

6

Bro. Herriman (A) for the Committee on Unfinished Business, read the
following extract from a letter from Bro. Albert P .Jacobs, Chairman Of the

Committee on the Eitual, dated February 22, 1887: 

'
'I have little to add in the matter of the Eitual. It has been impossible
for me to do much my time has been wholly taken up, and Coffin (Phi. 82),

upon whose ingenuity I greatly relied, is unable to spare any time at aU I
am greatly disgusted at this failure, and at my own inability to get more than

twenty four hours out of the day, "but so it is." I had hoped to finish a
simple outUne for lodgs exercises, yet even this I could not do. The fact is
that when my eyes went back on me in 1884 and again in 1886, my days for
outside work departed, I fear for a long period. As present my labors in a
legal and literary way are numerous and extensive, several years wiU be required
to conclude what I have on hand, and I see no chance for my completing the
Eitual unless some hard-working and ingenious brother settles down in my vi
cinity and urges the matter on to a speedy settlement. This is of course a very
informal report, but I beg you wiU use this letter to prevent my receiving
what the face of the record shows I richly deserve, a resolution of censure.
Against the passage of such a resolution, I could only urge that had I never
been i terested in the Fraternity, I should not have incapacitated myself to
work for it. If any brother will take up the Ritual matter he is welcome to
aU the suggestions and advice this part of the old committee can give.

The Committee on Unfinished Business recommended the abandonment
of the entire project of the Ritual. On motion of Bro. Bangs (A) the report
was unanimously approved and the recommendation adopted.
Bro. Herriman (A) offered Special Resolution Nos. 4 and 5, which were

unanimously adopted.

Bro. Burpee (K) offered Special Eesolution No. 7, which was unani
mously adopted.

GENERAL CONVENTION IN THE FIFTY-FOURTH

The Council is unable to present a
table of membership in the usual form, because of the failure on the part of
some of the chapters to render their annual reports, which were due on No
vember 1, 1886. No Chapter rendered its report for the past year at the time
required by the constitution.

Convention of 1883, was notified of the adoption of Gen. Res. No. VIII, of

The Diamond. 
In accordance with the instructions of General Resoluion No. XI, of 1886, the Council secured from Bro. AUison
George F. on

May 29, 1886, an assignment and transfer of all his right and interest in the
Diaiuond, including the copyright. As part of the consideration for the as
signment, the Council agreed to pay to Brother AUison "out of the net
profits arising out of the pubUcation of the Diamond in the years 1886 and
1887, included within the period of the publication of Volume, VI of the Dia
mond, the sum of one hundred aud eighty-two and 16-100 doUars," for the
purpose of paying outstanding debts, of which sum the CouncU has paid in ad
vance to Brother AUison $62.50, receiving his personal obligation for re-pay

ment, in case the expected profits prove insufficient to cover the advance.
In June, 1886, the CouncU appointed Brother H. L. Bridgman manager of
the Diamond for the ensuing year, subject to the Council's direction.
About September 1st, circulars announcing the assumption of the publication
by the Council, offering prizes for articles and for clubs, and inviting the co
operation of the Fraternity, were mailed to aU the Chapters. Publication of
the first number was fixed for November 1st, upon which date the editor had
in hand articles specially prepared and accepted, aggregating about 40,000
words and ample for a complete number; ten Chapter letters; 183 subscriptions, i

and $27 in money. As this was not deemed sufficientencouragement to en
gage in an enterprise requiring an outlay of at least $1,200, the $27 was re
turned to those who had paid it, and the Chapters advised that the Couucil,
in view of all the facts and the heavy expense to which the Fraternity was

already committed in the Catalogue, deemed it best to postpone further action
upon the Diamond until the meeting of the Convention.
A conditional offer to continue the publication was subsequently made by a
committee representing the Theta Chapter, but the near approach of the Con
vention seemed to render its acceptance inadvisable.
The CouncU has incurred no expense on account of the Diamond during the

past year. Since the postponement of pubUcation three more chapter letters

Song Book. In May, 1886, the CouncU appointed Brother W. D. Holmes
(X, '81), a committee to revise the Song Boot, but the appointment was decUned, and no progress has been made. The sales of the Song Book continue
to diminish. One copy has been sold and paid for during the past year. It is

Meeting of Featebnities. 
In May, 1886, certain members of the Frater
nity residing at or near Buffalo, N. Y., invited the opinion of the Council con
cerning a general meeting of coUege fraternity men, proposed to be held at
Lake Chautauqua in August. The Council, in response, having referred the
Brothers to Special Resolution No. 7, of 1883, the project was abandoned.
Printed copies of the correspondence relating to the matter were. distributed
throughout the Fraternity, and a copy is herewith submitted to the Conven
tion.
The Omega Chapteb. 
The University of Chicago having ceased to exist,
the Council has to announce that the Omega Chapter has likewise dissolved.
Its archives are in possession of the Council.
Finances. 
The Convention is referred to the Treasurer's Eeport herewith
Submitted for the details of the financial condition of the Fraternity. The
CouncU has on hand and on deposit money to the amount of $981,86.

12

The tax of 25 cents per active member authorized by Gen. Bes. No. Ill, of
1886, has not been called for, the Council being of the opinion that the high
rate of taxation for the year rendered it inexpedient to incur the expense
for which the special tax was authorized.

Taxes are still due from the Zeta, Psi and Beta Beta Chapters.
As far as the Council can now determine, no special taxes need be levied
for the coming year.

In Memobiam. Among the Fraternity dead of the past year are three

members of the Theta, whose memory wUl ever be cherished in our chapters:
Charles Washington Harvey.(Thefa,'37), one of the founders of the Fraternity,
died at r.uffalo, N. Y., October 15, 1886; Chester Alan Arthur (Theta, '48), at
New York City, November 18, 1886; and at Middletown, N. Y., December 18,
1886, WilUam Taylor (Theta, '38), the first freshman initiated into Psi UpsUon,
and associate founder of the Delta and the Lambda. Each of these brethren
merited and received the respect and confidence of the communities in which
'

they lived and labored, and by one was worthily sustained the honor and
the responsibility of the highest office in our country's gift. The Council
suggests that the Convention record its sense of the loss to the Fraternity
by the death of these eminent members, its appreciation of their lives and
character, and commend to the Chapters emulation of those qualities which
brought honor to them and upon the Fraternity.
